name: Clinical intake
summary: A streamed clinical note where a national identifier must never reach the screen, the log, or the chart, and a person accepts before anything is written.

brief.whoIsAsking: A clinician typing a situation and reading the note as it streams, who accepts the note before anything is written to the chart.
brief.whatTheyNeedBack: A streamed note with no national identifier ever shown, an email anonymized rather than deleted so the sentence still makes sense, and nothing written to the chart until they accept.
brief.systemsAlreadyRunning: A chart system of record that a person writes to on acceptance. An auditor later asks which user invoked the model and which chart excerpt a sentence came from. This is not a model-training project.
brief.breaksWhen: The identifier reaches the screen, the log, or the chart. It cannot be unseen, and a filter applied after the fact is an admission the requirement was never met.
brief.doneMeans: The identifier never appears in the stream, the email is anonymized rather than deleted, the chart updates only after a person accepts, and an auditor can tie the call to a user and a source excerpt.

steps.title: Content filters, a denied topic, and word filters
steps.decision: Which guardrail policies cover which risks, and why the identifier is not one a word filter can catch.
steps.why: A guardrail layers several policies, each for a different risk. Content filters cover categories (hate, violence, sexual, misconduct) by classification. A denied topic blocks a subject you define in natural language. Word filters block exact strings policy can enumerate — profanity, a competitor name. The national identifier is none of these: it is a pattern, not a listable word, so a word filter cannot catch it and the next step's PII handling must. Configuration: the lesson is which policy covers which risk, and that the identifier needs a different mechanism than a word list. The losing choice is trying to block the identifier with a word filter, which cannot enumerate every possible number.

snippets.label: A guardrail with content filters, a denied topic, and word filters — each for a different class of risk.

steps.infrastructure: // The guardrail layers policies by risk class: content filters classify categories, a denied topic blocks a subject defined in words, word filters block exact strings policy can enumerate. The national identifier is a pattern, not a listable word, so no word filter catches it — the next step's PII entity handling must. Each policy covers what the others cannot.

files.body:
The policies are not interchangeable. Content filters are classifiers over
categories; a denied topic is a natural-language subject boundary; word
filters are exact-string blocks. The identifier is the one that does not
fit any of them — you cannot list every national id number — which is
exactly why the PII entity policy (next steps) exists. Trying to force the
identifier into a word filter is the common mistake this step pre-empts.

checks.message: Content filters classify category risks (violence, hate, etc.) — the policy for things a classifier catches.
A denied topic blocks a subject defined in natural language — the policy for a boundary you describe rather than enumerate.
Word filters block exact strings policy can list. The identifier is not listable, so it is left to PII entity handling, not this policy.

steps.title: BLOCK the identifier, ANONYMIZE the email
steps.decision: Whether one PII action handles both the identifier and the email, or each gets the action its requirement needs.
steps.why: The requirements differ, so the actions differ. The national identifier must not appear at all — its PII entity is set to BLOCK, which stops the response rather than letting the value through in any form. The email can be replaced with a placeholder, because the rest of the sentence ('contact the patient at {EMAIL}') still has to make sense — its entity is set to ANONYMIZE, which masks the value while keeping the sentence usable. One action cannot do both jobs: BLOCK the email and you lose the sentence; ANONYMIZE the identifier and a masked-but-present value is still an admission it was there. Configuration: the lesson is per-entity actions. The losing choice is one blanket action for all PII.

snippets.label: Per-entity PII actions: BLOCK the identifier, ANONYMIZE the email. The requirement picks the action.

steps.infrastructure: // The identifier's PII entity is BLOCK — the response is stopped rather than letting the value through. The email's is ANONYMIZE — masked to a placeholder so 'contact the patient at {EMAIL}' still reads. One blanket action cannot serve both: BLOCK the email and the sentence breaks; ANONYMIZE the identifier and a masked-but-present value is still an admission it was there.

files.body:
BLOCK and ANONYMIZE are different promises. BLOCK stops the whole response
if the entity appears — the right action for something that must never be
seen in any form. ANONYMIZE replaces the value with a typed placeholder
and lets the response through — right for something the sentence needs
structurally but not literally. The identifier and the email have opposite
requirements, so they get opposite actions; a single action fails one of
them.

checks.message: The identifier's entity is BLOCK: the response is stopped, so the value never appears in any form.
The email's entity is ANONYMIZE: masked to a placeholder so the sentence still reads, rather than blocked.
PII actions are set per entity type, so the identifier and the email each get the action its requirement needs.

steps.title: Contextual grounding against the chart
steps.decision: Whether the note is checked for grounding against the chart excerpts, and at what threshold.
steps.why: A fluent note that is not supported by the chart is a confabulation in a medical record — the worst kind of wrong. Contextual grounding checks the generated note against the retrieved chart excerpts: it scores how much of the note is actually supported by the source, and blocks or flags a note that drifts beyond it. Thresholds start near 0.7 and tune — too high blocks good notes, too low lets unsupported claims through. Configuration: the lesson is the grounding policy against the chart, with a starting threshold. The losing choice is no grounding check, which lets a plausible-sounding but unsupported sentence into a clinical note the clinician may accept under time pressure.

snippets.label: A contextual grounding filter against the chart excerpts, with a starting threshold near 0.7.

steps.infrastructure: // Contextual grounding scores the note against the retrieved chart excerpts and blocks a note that drifts beyond what the source supports. Thresholds start near 0.7 and tune: too high blocks good notes, too low lets unsupported claims through. A fluent, unsupported sentence in a clinical record is the confabulation this catches.

files.body:
Grounding needs the sources tagged so the filter knows what the note is
meant to be supported by — the chart excerpts are the grounding source, the
note is the thing checked. The 0.7 start is a convention, not a law; the
right value comes from tuning against real notes. This is the same
contextual-grounding policy the policy assistant uses, here on a medical
record where an unsupported claim is especially dangerous.

checks.message: A grounding filter scores the note against the chart excerpts, catching a note that drifts beyond the source.
The threshold starts near 0.7 and is tuned — too high blocks good notes, too low lets unsupported claims through.
Grounding is a guardrail policy against the retrieved chart, so an unsupported sentence is caught before the clinician accepts it.

steps.title: ApplyGuardrail before any model call
steps.decision: Whether the guardrail runs on the input before the model, or only on the output after.
steps.why: The requirement is that the model must not see the raw identifier — not that the output is filtered. A filter on the output is too late: the model already received the identifier, and the invocation log already holds it. ApplyGuardrail runs the guardrail on the input text as a standalone call, before any model call, so a note containing the identifier is blocked before the model (or the log) ever sees it. This is runnable: ApplyGuardrail on input with a blocked entity returns a GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED action. The losing choice is relying only on output filtering, which cannot meet 'the model must not see the raw value' — by the time the output is filtered, the model saw it and the log recorded it.

snippets.label: ApplyGuardrail on the input as a standalone pre-check, before any model call.
snippets.source:
import boto3

runtime = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")

out = runtime.apply_guardrail(
    guardrailIdentifier="GR12345678",
    guardrailVersion="3",
    source="INPUT",
    content=[{"text": {"text": note_with_identifier, "qualifiers": ["guard_content"]}}],
)
print(out["action"])  # GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED when the identifier is present

snippets.label: From the terminal, confirm the guardrail and version exist before the pre-check depends on them — get-guardrail shows its status.
snippets.source: aws bedrock get-guardrail --guardrail-identifier GR12345678 --guardrail-version 3

steps.infrastructure: // ApplyGuardrail runs the guardrail on the input as a standalone call before any model call, so a note containing the identifier is blocked before the model or the log sees it. Output-only filtering is too late for 'the model must not see the raw value' — by then the model received it and the invocation log recorded it.

files.body:
# Assemble the ApplyGuardrail pre-check from the snippets on the left, then
# Run. The intercept returns GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED for a note with the
# identifier.
#
# The goal: the guardrail runs on the input before any model call, so the
# model never sees the raw identifier.

ApplyGuardrail is the independent guardrail API: it evaluates text without
a model call, which is exactly what 'the model must not see the raw value'
requires. The action field is NONE or GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED. This is the
pre-check; the next step applies the guardrail on the live chat turn too.
Both matter — the pre-check keeps the identifier out of the model and the
log, the chat-turn guardrail covers the generated output.

outputs.text: The note contains a blocked identifier and was stopped before the model call.

steps.title: guardrailConfig on the live chat turn
steps.decision: Whether the chat turn carries its own guardrailConfig, or the pre-check is assumed to cover the generated output too.
steps.why: The pre-check (ApplyGuardrail on input) covers what goes in; it does not cover what the model generates. The live Converse turn carries its own guardrailConfig so the output is evaluated too — a generated sentence that drifts off the chart, or somehow surfaces a value, is caught on the way out. This is the live call, not a second copy of the pre-check: the pre-check guards the input as a standalone step, the guardrailConfig guards the generation inline. This is runnable: Converse with guardrailConfig returns a response assessed by the guardrail. The losing choice is assuming the input pre-check covers the output, leaving the generated note unguarded.

snippets.label: The chat turn carries guardrailConfig, so the generated output is evaluated, not only the input.
snippets.source:
import boto3

runtime = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")

out = runtime.converse(
    modelId="eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": safe_input, "guardContent": {}}]}],
    guardrailConfig={"guardrailIdentifier": "GR12345678", "guardrailVersion": "3"},
)
print(out["stopReason"])

snippets.label: From the terminal, list the models to confirm the Converse model id is callable with the guardrail attached.
snippets.source: aws bedrock list-foundation-models --by-output-modality TEXT

steps.infrastructure: // The Converse turn carries guardrailConfig so the generated output is evaluated, not only the input the pre-check handled. The pre-check guards what goes in as a standalone call; the guardrailConfig guards the generation inline. Assuming the input pre-check covers the output leaves the generated note unguarded.

files.body:
# Assemble the guarded chat turn from the snippets on the left, then Run.
# The intercept returns a response assessed by the guardrail.
#
# The goal: the live turn carries guardrailConfig, so the generated output
# is guarded in addition to the input pre-check.

Two applications of the same guardrail, two jobs. ApplyGuardrail on the
input (previous step) keeps the identifier out of the model. guardrailConfig
on the Converse turn evaluates the generation on the way out. They are not
redundant — one guards input, one guards output — and the requirement
needs both: the raw value out of the model, and the generated note checked
for grounding and leakage.

content.text: Patient reports a two-day history of fever; contact the patient at {EMAIL}.

steps.title: guardContent keeps the trusted text out
steps.decision: Which parts of the prompt the guardrail evaluates, and why the system instruction is not one of them.
steps.why: A guardrail should evaluate the untrusted content — the user text, the tool results, the retrieved chunks — not your own trusted system instruction. Marking the untrusted parts with guardContent tells the guardrail what to assess; the system prompt is left out because guarding your own instruction throws away the turn: the guardrail may object to the very text that tells it how to behave, or waste the evaluation on content that was never the risk. Configuration: the lesson is scoping the guard to untrusted content. The losing choice is guarding everything including the system prompt, which both wastes evaluation and can trip the guardrail on its own instructions.

snippets.label: Mark the untrusted content with guardContent; leave the trusted system instruction unmarked.

steps.infrastructure: // guardContent marks the untrusted content — user text, tool results, retrieved chunks — as what the guardrail evaluates. The trusted system instruction is left unmarked, because guarding your own instruction wastes the evaluation on text that was never the risk and can trip the guardrail on its own behavior-defining prompt.

files.body:
guardContent is how you scope a guardrail to the risky parts. The threat is
in the user's input, the retrieved chunks (indirect injection), and tool
results — not in your own system prompt, which you wrote and trust. Marking
everything including the system text means the guardrail evaluates its own
instructions, which wastes the check and can cause spurious interventions.
Guard the untrusted, trust the trusted.

checks.message: The untrusted user text and chunks are marked with guardContent, so the guardrail evaluates them.
The system instruction is left unmarked, because guarding your own trusted instruction throws away the turn.
The retrieved chunks are guarded too, since indirect injection rides in the corpus, not only the user's text.

steps.title: sync on the stream, not async
steps.decision: Whether the streaming guardrail runs in sync mode, evaluating before tokens reach the clinician, or async.
steps.why: The clinician is reading the note as it streams. In async mode the guardrail evaluates chunks in the background while tokens are already on screen — so the identifier would be emitted and then flagged, and the clinician would already have read it. The requirement is that the identifier never appears, which only sync mode can meet: sync evaluates each chunk before it is released to the stream, holding a chunk until the guardrail clears it. Configuration: the lesson is streamProcessingMode SYNC. The losing choice is async for lower latency, which trades the one guarantee the scenario cannot give up — the identifier reaching the screen is the Breaks when.

snippets.label: Sync stream processing, so each chunk is evaluated before it reaches the clinician.

steps.infrastructure: // streamProcessingMode sync evaluates each chunk before it is released to the stream, holding it until the guardrail clears it. async evaluates in the background while tokens are already on screen — the identifier would be emitted and then flagged, which the clinician has already read. sync is the only mode that meets 'the identifier never appears.'

files.body:
sync vs async streaming is a latency-vs-safety trade, and here safety is
non-negotiable. async lets tokens flow and checks them in parallel, lower
latency but the chunk is already visible when flagged. sync holds each
chunk for evaluation before release, slightly slower but the identifier is
never on screen. For a requirement phrased as 'never appears,' async is
disqualified — it appears, then disappears, and appearing was the failure.

checks.message: Sync stream processing evaluates each chunk before release, so the identifier is cleared before the clinician can read it.
A chunk is held until the guardrail clears it, which is what 'the identifier never appears' requires.
Not async. Async emits the chunk and flags it after — the clinician has already read the identifier, which is the Breaks when.

steps.title: Guardrail trace off in production
steps.decision: Whether guardrail trace stays on in production, given the trace records the sensitive span it matched.
steps.why: Guardrail trace is how you debug why the guardrail intervened — it returns the matched span, which for this guardrail is the national identifier it just blocked. So the trace is the one place the identifier leaves after you blocked it in the answer: you stopped it reaching the clinician, then logged it in the trace. Trace is on in dev to tune the guardrail and off in production. Configuration: the lesson is guardrail trace off in production. The losing choice is leaving trace on, which re-introduces the exact value the guardrail exists to suppress, into the logs, after every intervention.

snippets.label: Guardrail trace enabled only outside production. The trace holds the matched identifier.

steps.infrastructure: // Guardrail trace returns the matched span — the identifier the guardrail just blocked — so leaving it on in production re-introduces the exact value you suppressed, into the logs, after every intervention. Trace is on in dev to tune the guardrail and off in production. It is the one place a blocked value leaks back.

files.body:
The recurring trace rule, at its sharpest here. A guardrail that blocks an
identifier then writes that identifier into its trace has moved the leak,
not closed it. On in dev, off in prod. The same discipline as the member-
services agent trace and the policy assistant's guardrail trace: the trace
is a debugging aid that necessarily contains the sensitive thing it traced.

checks.message: Guardrail trace is disabled in production, so the matched identifier does not leave via the trace.
Trace is on in dev to tune and off in prod, because the trace holds the identifier the guardrail blocked.
Trace is not hardcoded on. It is tied to the stage, so production gets it off and the blocked value does not leak back.

steps.title: Comprehend, Macie, and the guardrail each do one job
steps.decision: Which PII tool covers which surface — text the pipeline submits, data at rest, and the inference call — and why none replaces the others.
steps.why: Three tools, three surfaces. Comprehend detects PII entities in text your pipeline submits — a batch of notes, a document you are about to process. Macie scans what is already in an S3 bucket — data at rest you did not inspect on the way in. The guardrail is the inference-time check on the model's input and output. None replaces the others: Comprehend does not watch the bucket, Macie does not run inline, the guardrail does not scan storage. This is runnable: Comprehend detect_pii_entities returns the entities in submitted text. The losing choice is assuming one of them covers all three surfaces, leaving a gap — PII at rest, in flight, or at inference — uncovered.

snippets.label: Comprehend detects PII entities in text the pipeline submits. One of three surfaces.
snippets.source:
import boto3

comprehend = boto3.client("comprehend", region_name="eu-central-1")

out = comprehend.detect_pii_entities(
    Text="Contact the patient at a.nordheim@example.com regarding SIN 123-456-789.",
    LanguageCode="en",
)
for e in out["Entities"]:
    print(e["Type"], e["Score"])

snippets.label: From the terminal, check what Macie covers — list the classification jobs that scan data at rest, a different surface than Comprehend.
snippets.source: aws macie2 list-classification-jobs

steps.infrastructure: // Three PII surfaces, three tools: Comprehend detects entities in text the pipeline submits, Macie scans data already at rest in a bucket, and the guardrail is the inference-time check. None replaces the others — Comprehend does not watch storage, Macie does not run inline, the guardrail does not scan a bucket. A gap in any surface is uncovered PII.

files.body:
# Assemble the Comprehend PII detection from the snippets on the left, then
# Run. The intercept returns the entities found in the submitted text.
#
# The goal: Comprehend covers text the pipeline submits — one of three PII
# surfaces, alongside Macie (at rest) and the guardrail (at inference).

The exam trap is treating these as interchangeable 'PII tools.' They cover
different surfaces: Comprehend is detection in text you submit (in flight,
by your pipeline); Macie is discovery in S3 (at rest, often data you did
not inspect); the guardrail is the inline check on the model call. A design
that uses one and assumes it covers the others has an uncovered surface,
which for health data is a finding, not a gap you discover later.

steps.title: Mask before the prompt, not the output
steps.decision: Whether a value the model must never see is masked before the prompt, or filtered from the output after.
steps.why: When the requirement is 'the model must never see the raw value,' output filtering cannot meet it by definition — the model has already processed the value to produce the output you are filtering. Masking before the prompt replaces the raw value with a placeholder in the input, using Comprehend's detected offsets, so the model receives {SIN} and never the number. Output filtering is the right tool for 'do not show the value to the user'; masking-before-prompt is the tool for 'do not let the model see it.' This is runnable: masking the detected entities before the call sends a redacted prompt. The losing choice is output filtering for a never-see-it requirement, which is a filter applied after the model already saw the raw value.

snippets.label: Mask the detected entities in the input before the prompt, so the model receives placeholders, not raw values.
snippets.source:
def mask(text, entities):
    # entities from Comprehend, sorted by BeginOffset descending so
    # offsets stay valid as we replace.
    for e in sorted(entities, key=lambda x: x["BeginOffset"], reverse=True):
        text = text[: e["BeginOffset"]] + "{" + e["Type"] + "}" + text[e["EndOffset"] :]
    return text

masked_prompt = mask(raw_note, detected_entities)

snippets.label: From the terminal, confirm Comprehend is reachable for the detection the mask depends on — list its endpoints or a quick no-op.
snippets.source: aws comprehend list-pii-entities-detection-jobs

steps.infrastructure: // Masking replaces the raw value with a typed placeholder in the input before the prompt, using Comprehend's offsets, so the model receives {SIN} and never the number. Output filtering cannot meet 'the model must never see the raw value' — by the time you filter the output, the model processed the raw value to produce it. Mask input for never-see; filter output for never-show.

files.body:
# Assemble the input masking from the snippets on the left, then Run. The
# intercept confirms the detection the mask uses.
#
# The goal: raw values are masked to placeholders before the prompt, so the
# model never receives the identifier — output filtering is too late.

'Never see' and 'never show' are different requirements with different
tools. Never-show: filter or anonymize the output — the model saw the
value, the user does not. Never-see: mask the input before the prompt — the
model receives a placeholder. This clinical requirement is never-see (even
a later filter would have the log and the model exposure), so masking
before the prompt is the only mechanism that satisfies it. Comprehend finds
the spans; the mask replaces them before the call.

steps.title: Invocation logs hold the raw body, so encrypt
steps.decision: How the invocation logs are protected, given they contain the raw prompt and completion.
steps.why: Even with input masking and output filtering, the invocation log records the raw request and response body — 'we filtered the answer' is not 'the identifier is gone,' because the log is a separate surface that holds what the call carried. So the log group is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key (not the default AWS-managed one, so key access is yours to scope), readers are a short least-privilege list, and retention is set rather than never-expire. Configuration: the lesson is the CMK-encrypted, least-privilege, retention-bounded log group. The losing choice is default encryption and open read access on logs that contain exactly the PII the rest of the pipeline works to suppress.

snippets.label: The invocation log group encrypted with a customer-managed key, readers scoped, retention set.

steps.infrastructure: // The invocation log holds the raw prompt and completion, so 'we filtered the answer' is not 'the identifier is gone' — the log is a separate surface. It is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key (key access is yours to scope), readers are a short least-privilege list, and retention is bounded, not never-expire.

files.body:
The log is the surface people forget because the pipeline 'handled' the
PII. But invocation logging records the request and response bodies, which
are where the raw values lived before masking or after the model produced
them. A customer-managed key means you control who can decrypt, not just
AWS; the short reader list and bounded retention limit exposure and
lifetime. This is the same logging discipline as the policy assistant's
logging step, with the stakes raised to health data.

checks.message: The log group is encrypted with a customer-managed key, so decryption access is yours to scope — not the default AWS-managed key.
Retention is bounded, not never-expire, limiting how long the raw-body logs live.
Readers are a short, named least-privilege list, because the logs hold exactly the PII the pipeline works to suppress.

steps.title: Secrets Manager for the downstream token
steps.decision: Whether the downstream token lives in the system prompt or in Secrets Manager.
steps.why: The pipeline calls a downstream system that needs a token. Putting that token in the system prompt is a double mistake: the prompt is sent on every call and recorded in the invocation log, so the secret is now logged with every request — and the log already holds the raw body you are protecting. Secrets Manager holds the token, the handler fetches it at init, and it never enters the prompt or the log. Configuration: the lesson is the token in Secrets Manager, out of the prompt. The losing choice is a token in the system prompt, which logs a credential on every call in a pipeline whose whole point is not to leak sensitive values.

snippets.label: The downstream token in Secrets Manager, granted to the handler, never in the prompt.

steps.infrastructure: // The downstream token lives in Secrets Manager, fetched at init, never in the system prompt. A token in the prompt is sent and logged on every call — and this pipeline's invocation log already holds the raw body. Putting a credential there logs it with every request, in the one system built to not leak sensitive values.

files.body:
The system prompt feels like a convenient place for configuration, and a
token is configuration, so it slips in. But the prompt is logged with every
invocation — especially here, where invocation logging is on — so a token
in the prompt is a credential written to CloudWatch on every call. Secrets
Manager keeps it out of the prompt and the log. Same lesson as the contract
desk's credential step, sharpened by the logging in this pipeline.

checks.message: The downstream token is held in Secrets Manager, fetched at init rather than carried in the prompt.
The environment holds the secret's ARN; the token is resolved at runtime, not placed in the system prompt.
The token is not concatenated into the system prompt. A prompt-embedded token is logged with every call — the leak this avoids.

steps.title: CloudTrail data events for InvokeModel
steps.decision: Whether InvokeModel calls are captured as CloudTrail data events, or management events are assumed to record them.
steps.why: The auditor asks which user invoked the model. CloudTrail management events record control-plane actions — creating a guardrail, changing a config — but they do not record every InvokeModel call. The model invocation is a data event, and data events are off by default and configured per resource. So the trail explicitly enables Bedrock data events, and now every call carries the identity that made it. Configuration: the lesson is the data-event selector for InvokeModel. The losing choice is relying on management events, which answer 'who changed the guardrail' but not 'who invoked the model on this patient,' leaving the auditor's actual question unanswerable.

snippets.label: A CloudTrail data-event selector for Bedrock model invocation, so every InvokeModel call records its caller.

steps.infrastructure: // Model invocation is a CloudTrail data event, off by default and configured per resource. Management events record control-plane changes (who edited the guardrail), not every InvokeModel call. The trail enables Bedrock data events so each call records its caller — which is exactly the auditor's 'which user invoked the model' question.

files.body:
The management-vs-data-event distinction is the whole step. Management
events are the default and cover API calls that change configuration. Data
events cover the high-volume data-plane operations — S3 object access,
Lambda invokes, Bedrock model invocations — and are opt-in per resource
because they are voluminous. The auditor's 'who invoked the model' is a
data-event question; a trail of management events alone cannot answer it.

checks.message: A data-event selector is configured, so high-volume data-plane calls are captured, not only management events.
The selector captures data events for Bedrock, so each InvokeModel call records the identity that made it.
Every model invocation records its caller, which answers the auditor's 'which user invoked the model' — a data-event question.

steps.title: Augmented AI gates the chart write
steps.decision: Whether the chart is written on model output, or only after a person accepts through an Augmented AI review.
steps.why: Until the clinician accepts, the chart does not change. Augmented AI (A2I) is the human-review gate: the generated note goes to a review task, the clinician accepts (or edits, or rejects), and only an accepted note is written to the chart. The write is downstream of the acceptance, not of the model. This is distinct from Ground Truth, which is a labeling path for building a training dataset — a different job entirely, and not a gate on this chart. Configuration: the lesson is A2I as the acceptance gate before the system of record. The losing choice is writing the chart on model output with review bolted on after, which means the chart changed before the person accepted.

snippets.label: An Augmented AI human-review flow gating the chart write. Only an accepted note is written.

steps.infrastructure: // Augmented AI is the acceptance gate: the generated note goes to a human-review task, the clinician accepts, and only then is the note written to the chart. The write is downstream of acceptance, not model output. Ground Truth is a labeling path for training data — a different job, not a gate on this chart.

files.body:
A2I (Augmented AI) and Ground Truth both involve humans, which is why they
are confused. Ground Truth labels data to train a model — not relevant
here, this is not a training project. A2I inserts a human-review loop into
an inference pipeline, which is exactly the accept-before-write gate the
clinician requires. The chart being downstream of acceptance, not model
output, is the structural form of 'until they accept, the chart does not
change.'

checks.message: An Augmented AI flow definition inserts a human-review loop, so the chart write waits on a clinician's acceptance.
The chart write is downstream of acceptance, not model output — nothing reaches the chart until the clinician accepts.
No Ground Truth labeling job. That is a training-data path, not the acceptance gate this chart needs.

steps.title: A model card and a sliced eval
steps.decision: How the system's evaluation is documented and sliced, and when SageMaker Clarify applies.
steps.why: A clinical system needs its evaluation documented and sliced, not reduced to one aggregate score. A model card records the intended use, the data, the limits, and the eval results. The eval is sliced by the groups you are permitted to measure, because an aggregate accuracy can hide a subgroup where the system is worse. SageMaker Clarify is the bias/explainability tool when the comparison is a classic ML model with features and labels — it is not the right tool for a Bedrock chat evaluation, which is scored on generation quality and safety, not feature attributions. Configuration: the lesson is the model card plus sliced eval, and Clarify scoped to classic models. The losing choice is a single aggregate score with no slices and Clarify pointed at a chat model it does not fit.

files.body:
Two things to get right. Slicing: an aggregate accuracy can be fine overall
and poor for one age band or language, which in a clinical system is a
safety and fairness problem a single number hides. The model card is where
the intended use and limits are stated so the system is not used outside
them. Clarify's scope: it explains and measures bias in classic ML models
with features and labels — it does not evaluate a Bedrock chat, which needs
generation-quality and safety evals instead.

checks.message: A model card documents intended use, data, limits, and results — the system's evaluation is recorded, not implicit.
The eval is sliced by permitted groups, so a subgroup where the system is worse is not hidden by an aggregate score.
Clarify is scoped to a classic model with features and labels, not the Bedrock chat — which is scored on generation quality and safety.

steps.title: Jailbreak and false-refusal sets, calibrated judge
steps.decision: What the safety eval in the pipeline measures, and whether a judge model can gate a deploy before it is calibrated.
steps.why: Two safety eval sets, not one. A jailbreak set checks the guardrail is not talked around — prompts that try to extract the identifier or bypass the filters. A false-refusal set checks the guardrail is not so aggressive it refuses legitimate clinical content — a note mentioning a condition is not an attack. Both run in the pipeline and gate the deploy. A judge model can score them, but only after it is calibrated against a human-labeled sample — an uncalibrated judge that over- or under-flags cannot be trusted to block a release. Configuration: the lesson is the two safety sets plus the calibrated judge. The losing choice is a jailbreak set alone (ships an over-refusing system) or an uncalibrated judge gating deploys on scores nobody validated.

snippets.label: Jailbreak and false-refusal sets in the pipeline, scored by a judge calibrated on a human sample first.

steps.infrastructure: // Two safety sets gate the deploy: a jailbreak set (the guardrail is not talked around) and a false-refusal set (the guardrail does not refuse legitimate clinical content). A judge model scores them only after calibration against a human-labeled sample — an uncalibrated judge that over- or under-flags cannot be trusted to block a release.

files.body:
Safety eval has two failure directions, and measuring only one ships the
other. Jailbreak: the system can be talked past its guardrail. False
refusal: the guardrail is so strict it refuses legitimate clinical content,
which in this setting means refusing to help with a real note. Both gate
the pipeline. The judge-model caveat is the calibration: a judge is cheap
and biased toward its own style, so it is calibrated on a human-labeled
sample before it is trusted to block a deploy — the same discipline as the
policy assistant's eval judge.

checks.message: A jailbreak set checks the guardrail cannot be talked around — the extract-the-identifier direction.
A false-refusal set checks the guardrail does not refuse legitimate clinical content — the over-strict direction a jailbreak-only eval misses.
The judge model is calibrated on a human-labeled sample before it gates a deploy — an uncalibrated judge cannot be trusted to block a release.
